proposed_title: Kennedy says HHS expects to identify cause of autism increase by September and focuses on environmental factors
description_short: Kennedy says HHS expects to identify cause of autism increase by September and focuses on environmental factors
description_medium: In April 2025, HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said a federal effort would identify the cause of the rise in autism diagnoses by September. He emphasized investigation of environmental contributors. The record should not attribute the specific processed-food, seed-oil and pesticide causal formulation without a direct source.
description_long:
On April 10, 2025, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said the United States would know the cause of what he called the autism “epidemic” by September, according to the supplied contemporaneous Reuters report. The claim concerned an expected federal effort to investigate the rise in autism diagnoses. The supplied synopsis says Kennedy emphasized environmental contributors, but it does not establish that he identified a particular environmental factor as the cause.

That distinction matters because the original framing attributed a specific causal claim involving processed food, seed oils and pesticides to Kennedy. The supplied correction explicitly says the located reporting does not support that combined formulation or the original March timing. The record is therefore narrowed to the documented September deadline and focus on environmental factors, rather than repeating unverified specifics. The statement was a prediction about what HHS expected to determine, not evidence that the cause had already been established. The supplied information does not say whether the effort met its deadline, what methods it used, or what conclusions it reached. It also does not provide evidence that environmental factors explain the increase in diagnoses. The supported consequence is that Kennedy publicly set an expectation for a federal answer by September 2025, creating a clear benchmark against which later findings could be assessed; the accuracy and outcome of that prediction are not established here.

supports: On April 10, 2025, Kennedy said the administration expected to identify a cause of the reported rise in autism diagnoses by September and described an investigation into environmental factors.
support.access_note: Contemporaneous Reuters report reviewed; supports the forecast and timing, not a specific causal finding.

evidence_gaps: The report does not support the original March date or the specific processed-food, seed-oil and pesticide claim. The September statement was a forecast, not evidence that a cause was identified.

proposed_title: Trump Administration Withholds Title X Funds From Nine Planned Parenthood Affiliates
description_short: Planned Parenthood said nine affiliates were told Title X family-planning funds would be withheld beginning April 1, 2025.
description_medium: On March 31, 2025, Planned Parenthood said nine affiliates had been notified that federal Title X family-planning funds would be withheld starting April 1. Reuters reported the notice as a program-specific funding freeze. It does not show that the administration ended every form of federal funding to Planned Parenthood nationwide, including all Medicaid reimbursements, or that every Title X grant was terminated.
description_long:
On March 31, 2025, Planned Parenthood said the administration had notified nine of its affiliates that their federal Title X family-planning funding would be withheld beginning the next day. Reuters reported the organization’s account of the notice. Title X supports family-planning services, but this report concerns a funding action affecting nine affiliates; it does not establish that every Planned Parenthood affiliate lost all federal support.

The original card described a February nationwide termination of all federal funding, including Medicaid reimbursements. The cited report does not substantiate that scope or date. The described Title X freeze should also remain distinct from later Medicaid restrictions, which involve a different funding mechanism and timeline. The available source documents the notice and its scheduled start, not the ultimate duration of the freeze, the amount withheld from each affiliate, or service losses at individual clinics. The corrected account therefore records the reported program and affected group while avoiding a claim of nationwide defunding. Further detail about the implementation and effects would require additional reporting beyond this source.

proposed_title: Trump orders federal steps restricting support for gender-affirming care for minors
corrected_claim: Trump signed Executive Order 14187 on January 28, 2025. It directs specified federal agencies to take steps concerning federal support for defined gender-transition procedures for people under 19, subject to applicable law. The order is not evidence that every provider immediately stopped care or that patients experienced a uniform outcome.
description_short: EO 14187 directs federal actions concerning specified gender-affirming care for people under 19, subject to law.
description_medium: Trump signed Executive Order 14187 on January 28, 2025. It directs specified federal agencies to take steps concerning federal support for defined gender-transition procedures for people under 19, subject to applicable law. The order is not evidence that every provider immediately stopped care or that patients experienced a uniform outcome.
description_long: President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14187, “Protecting Children from Chemical and Surgical Mutilation,” on January 28, 2025. The order defines children as people under 19 and directs federal agencies to take specified steps concerning funding, federal programs, research, and agency policy related to defined gender-transition procedures. The directives are qualified by applicable law and depend on agency implementation. The order does not itself show that every health-care provider stopped offering care, that a nationwide provider ban took effect immediately, or what happened to any particular patient. This entry should describe the executive action and its stated mechanisms rather than assume uniform implementation or patient effects. The title’s original timing of January 20 is incorrect; that date is associated with other executive actions, while this order was signed January 28. Any statement about injunctions, later enforcement, or access to care in a particular state requires a separate source describing the relevant legal proceeding or provider. The cited order supports the federal directive and its limits, not downstream outcomes.

frozen_original.synopsis: On January 20, 2025, Trump signed an executive order directing all federal agencies, federally funded programs, and military healthcare facilities to cease providing gender-affirming care to anyone under 19 years of age, including puberty blockers and hormone therapy that major medical organizations including the American Medical Association, American Academy of Pediatrics, and American Psychological Association consider medically necessary treatments for adolescents with gender dysphoria. proposed_title: Agencies Pause Enforcement of New 2024 Mental Health Parity Rule Provisions
description_short: Agencies paused enforcement of new 2024 parity-rule provisions; MHPAEA’s statutory duties and 2013 rule remained in effect.
description_medium: On May 15, 2025, the Departments of Labor, HHS and Treasury said they would not enforce requirements newly added by the 2024 Mental Health Parity final rule while related litigation proceeded and for 18 months after a final decision. The agencies said MHPAEA’s statutory obligations and the 2013 rule remained in effect. This was a limited enforcement pause, not a repeal of parity law or an end to all enforcement.
description_long: On May 15, 2025, the Departments of Labor, Health and Human Services, and the Treasury announced that they would not enforce provisions newly added by the 2024 final rule implementing the Mental Health Parity and Addiction Equity Act (MHPAEA) while related litigation was pending and for 18 months after a final decision. The agencies explicitly said that MHPAEA’s statutory requirements and the earlier 2013 rule remained in effect. The announcement therefore changed the enforcement status of newer requirements; it did not repeal the parity statute, end every parity obligation or make insurers free of all requirements. The original entry gives the wrong date and overstates the action as an end to parity enforcement. The agencies’ statement does not establish that insurers then changed specific coverage practices, narrowed particular networks or denied treatment to a stated number of people. Those effects would need separate evidence. The supported correction is limited to the scope and timing of the announced pause and the obligations the agencies said continued to apply; the source does not establish the later outcome of litigation or reconsideration.

proposed_title: Trump Administration Announces Review of About $9 Billion in Harvard Funding
description_short: On March 31, 2025, the administration announced a review of about $9 billion in Harvard federal grants and contracts, citing antisemitism allegations.
description_medium: On March 31, 2025, the Trump administration announced a review of roughly $9 billion in federal grants and contracts to Harvard, citing allegations of antisemitism. The reported amount was funding under review, not money canceled that day. This was a March review; broader policy demands and a funding freeze were later developments, not a February threat combined with the review.
description_long: On March 31, 2025, the Trump administration announced that it would review roughly $9 billion in federal grants and contracts to Harvard, citing allegations of antisemitism. The figure described the value of funding under review; the announcement did not say that $9 billion had already been canceled. The date and scope correct the original entry, which described a February letter and combined the review with a list of university-governance demands. Those are not established by the cited March 31 report. Broader demands and a funding freeze were later developments, but they are separate actions and should not be collapsed into the March review or assigned the same date. The available source does not identify which individual grants or contracts were affected, what amount was ultimately canceled, or the outcome of each funding decision. The supported event is the dated announcement of a review, its approximate funding scope, and the administration's stated rationale—not a completed $9 billion cut or a February ultimatum.

proposed_title: Trump Orders Federal DEI Programs Closed and Staff Placed on Leave
description_short: A January 20 executive order directed federal agencies to end DEI programs and close offices; Education later reported placing its DEI staff on paid leave.
description_medium: Executive Order 14151, signed January 20, 2025, directed federal agencies to terminate DEI programs and close DEI offices, and provided for affected employees to be placed on paid leave. On January 23, the Education Department said it had put employees leading DEI initiatives on leave and dissolved its Diversity and Inclusion Council. These sources do not establish a universal shutdown of university offices.
description_long:
On January 20, 2025, President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14151, directing federal agencies to terminate federal diversity, equity, and inclusion programs and close DEI offices. The order also directed agencies to place employees working in affected programs on paid administrative leave while they took steps to close those programs.

On January 23, the Department of Education announced an agency-specific implementation step: employees leading its DEI initiatives were placed on paid leave, and the department dissolved its Diversity and Inclusion Council. These sources document an executive order and actions within one federal department. They do not show that all federal DEI employees were fired on January 20 or that every federally funded university immediately eliminated its chief diversity officer or closed its own office.

This correction replaces the earlier citation to a different executive order with the Federal Register record for Executive Order 14151, which is the order described here. It keeps the event focused on federal agency programs and the Education Department’s reported action. Claims about university-wide funding conditions, effects on workplace protections, or later legal outcomes require additional evidence and are not inferred from these two notices.

proposed_title: Trump Signed an Order Directing a K-12 Strategy on What It Called “Radical Indoctrination”
description_short: EO 14190, signed January 29, 2025, directed agencies to develop a federal strategy concerning K-12 schooling; it did not itself enact a nationwide curriculum ban.
description_medium: Executive Order 14190 was signed January 29, 2025, and titled “Ending Radical Indoctrination in K-12 Schooling.” It directs federal agencies to prepare an “Ending Indoctrination Strategy” within 90 days. The order’s terminology reflects the administration’s characterization; it does not itself ban the described lessons nationwide or establish funding conditions for universities.
description_long: President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14190 on January 29, 2025. The order, titled “Ending Radical Indoctrination in K-12 Schooling,” directed the Secretaries of Education, Defense, and Health and Human Services, in consultation with the Attorney General, to provide an “Ending Indoctrination Strategy” within 90 days. That is the discrete action supported by the Federal Register text. The original account uses January 20 as the date and imports “divisive concepts” language from a separate 2020 order. It also describes an immediate nationwide teaching ban, broad funding conditions for K-12 schools and universities, and reported teacher self-censorship; this order text does not establish those effects. The corrected entry uses the actual date, executive order number, stated title, and requested federal strategy. Phrases such as “radical indoctrination” are presented as the order’s characterization rather than an independent finding about school curricula. Any later agency implementation or legal challenge requires separate sources.

proposed_title: FY2026 Education Budget Proposes Pell, Work-Study and TRIO Cuts, Not an End to All Aid
description_short: The FY2026 Education request proposed cuts to Pell, Work-Study and TRIO, not an end to all federal student aid.
description_medium: The May 30, 2025, FY2026 Education budget request retained Pell Grants but proposed a $5,710 maximum award for 2026–27, $250 million for Federal Work-Study, no Supplemental Educational Opportunity Grant appropriation and no discretionary funding for TRIO. These were proposals, not enacted changes, and the request did not eliminate all federal student aid.
description_long: The Department of Education’s May 30, 2025, FY2026 budget request proposed major reductions to higher-education programs, but it did not eliminate all federal student aid. The request retained Pell Grant funding while proposing a maximum award of $5,710 for 2026–27, $1,685 below the 2024–25 maximum. It proposed $250 million for Federal Work-Study, a reduction of $980 million, no appropriation for Supplemental Educational Opportunity Grants (SEOG), and no discretionary funding for Federal TRIO programs. These figures describe the administration’s budget proposal, not amounts enacted by Congress. The request therefore called for substantial reductions and selected program eliminations while retaining Pell Grants and some work-study funding; it did not propose eliminating every federal student-aid program. The eventual effect depended on congressional action and implementation. The cited budget materials do not substantiate predictions about particular colleges or an ideological goal of ending the federal role in higher education. The supported event is the FY2026 proposal and its specific program changes.

proposed_title: Appeals Court Hears Challenge to Boasberg Contempt Inquiry Over Deportation Flights
description_short: The D.C. Circuit heard arguments on September 29, 2026, over Boasberg's contempt inquiry into March 2025 deportation flights.
description_medium: On September 29, 2026, a D.C. Circuit panel heard arguments over whether Judge James Boasberg's contempt inquiry into March 2025 deportation flights should continue. Boasberg found that officials acted in bad faith; the administration disputed the order's scope and appealed. As of October 3, 2026, the appeals court had issued no final ruling, so the dispute remained unresolved.
description_long: On September 29, 2026, a panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit heard arguments about Judge James Boasberg's contempt inquiry into the administration's handling of March 2025 deportation flights. Boasberg had found that officials acted in bad faith and began contempt proceedings after flights carrying Venezuelan nationals proceeded despite his direction to halt or return them. The administration disputed whether a binding order covered the flights and challenged the contempt inquiry on appeal. The parties' positions remained contested at the hearing. As of October 3, 2026, the appellate court had not issued a final decision. The record should describe this September 2026 appellate hearing and distinguish it from the March 15, 2025 flights that gave rise to the dispute. It should not present the judge's finding as an uncontested final determination or imply that the appeal had already been decided. The cited reporting documents the hearing and procedural posture at that date; a later ruling could change the case's status.

proposed_title: Supreme Court Sets Habeas Venue and Notice Rules in Alien Enemies Act Case
description_short: Supreme Court Sets Habeas Venue and Notice Rules in Alien Enemies Act Case
description_medium: In Trump v. J.G.G. on April 7, 2025, the Supreme Court said core habeas petitions belong in the district of confinement and required notice with a reasonable chance to seek habeas relief before removal. The decision addressed a particular Alien Enemies Act case; it did not eliminate federal courts’ jurisdiction over immigration cases generally.
description_long: In Trump v. J.G.G., decided April 7, 2025, the Supreme Court considered challenges to removals under the Alien Enemies Act. The Court said venue for core habeas petitions lies in the district where a person is confined; because the detainees were in Texas, the District of Columbia was not the proper venue for their habeas claims. The opinion also required the government to give notice within a reasonable time and in a way that allowed affected people to seek habeas relief in the proper venue before removal. This was a procedural ruling in a specific case and described a route for judicial review. It does not establish that federal courts lack authority over immigration cases generally, and the supplied record identifies no March guidance or bill that purported to remove that authority. The linked 2026 Reuters article reports a separate appellate dispute about deportation-flight compliance; it is not evidence of a general jurisdiction-stripping order.

proposed_title: Trump Orders Agencies to Identify Federal Funds for Suspension or Termination in Sanctuary Jurisdictions
description_short: Trump Orders Agencies to Identify Federal Funds for Suspension or Termination in Sanctuary Jurisdictions
description_medium: On April 28, 2025, Trump signed Executive Order 14287 directing the attorney general and Homeland Security secretary to identify states and localities the administration considers sanctuary jurisdictions. It directs agency heads, as permitted by law, to identify federal grants and contracts for possible suspension or termination for designated jurisdictions and directs legal measures against jurisdictions that remain in what the order calls defiance of federal law. The order does not state that jurisdictions are to be punished for complying with federal court orders against the administration.
description_long:
On April 28, 2025, President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14287 directing the attorney general and homeland security secretary to identify state and local governments the administration considered sanctuary jurisdictions. The order instructed agencies, where permitted by law, to identify federal grants and contracts that might be suspended or terminated for those jurisdictions. It also directed legal measures against jurisdictions the administration said were defying federal law. The order did not say that a jurisdiction should be punished for complying with a federal court order against the administration.

The directive sought to use federal funding and legal authority as pressure on local governments over immigration policy. Its effects depended on identifying grants, statutory authority, and later agency decisions; the order itself did not immediately cancel every grant. The distinction between a directive to review funding and an actual termination is important. The order directed agencies to review funding and pursue legal steps; it did not find that every listed jurisdiction had violated federal law.

does_not_support: Does not target compliance with court orders or itself terminate funds; later agency action is required.

description_long: On January 20, 2025, President Donald Trump issued a proclamation granting clemency for certain offenses relating to events at or near the U.S. Capitol on January 6, 2021. The Justice Department’s Office of the Pardon Attorney describes the action as presidential clemency and explains that its office can issue pardon certificates to people covered by the proclamation. The actor, date, legal mechanism, and scope are distinct from the earlier claim that Attorney General Pam Bondi directed the Justice Department to dismiss a broad set of pending cases on January 21. proposed_title: DOJ Orders Civil Rights Division to Pause Litigation Pending Review
description_short: A January 2025 DOJ memo paused Civil Rights Division cases and settlements for review; it did not show the division had shut down.
description_medium: Reuters reported that on January 22, 2025, the Justice Department ordered its Civil Rights Division to pause ongoing Biden-era litigation, bring no new cases, and agree to no settlements while matters were reviewed. The report describes a litigation-review directive, not a shutdown of the division. It does not support the claim that all senior leaders were placed on leave or that federal civil-rights enforcement ceased.
description_long:
On January 22, 2025, Reuters reported that the Justice Department had directed its Civil Rights Division to pause ongoing litigation inherited from the Biden administration, bring no new cases, and agree to no settlements while the matters were reviewed. The instruction temporarily restricted litigation and settlement activity as the department reconsidered cases from the previous administration.

The report supports describing a review directive and its effect on the division’s legal docket. It does not say that the division stopped operating, that every senior leader was placed on administrative leave on January 21, or that all federal enforcement of civil-rights laws ceased. A pause pending review also does not establish that each case was ultimately abandoned; the cited account does not provide the final outcome for every matter. Claims about specific voting-rights cases, police consent decrees, or other enforcement actions require separate evidence. This correction keeps the event to the documented litigation pause and avoids treating a temporary review as a final disposition or a complete institutional shutdown.

proposed_title: VA Limits New Cross-Sex Hormone Therapy for Gender Dysphoria While Allowing Some Existing Care
description_short: A March 2025 VA notice limited new cross-sex hormone therapy for gender dysphoria but allowed specified veterans to continue.
description_medium: On March 17, 2025, VA rescinded its prior transgender-care directive. Its notice limited cross-sex hormone therapy through VA to veterans already receiving it as of that date or receiving it at separation from military service, if otherwise eligible. VA said comprehensive health care, including preventive and mental-health care, would continue. The notice was not an immediate cancellation of every existing prescription.
description_long:
On March 17, 2025, the Veterans Health Administration rescinded its 2018 directive on care for transgender and intersex veterans. The new notice limited cross-sex hormone therapy through VA to veterans already receiving that care from VA on the notice date, or veterans for whom it was provided as part of and upon separation from military service, if otherwise eligible for VA health care. Veterans outside those exceptions were not eligible for the therapy through VA under the notice.

The policy therefore restricted access for new patients while allowing specified veterans to continue; it did not immediately cancel every existing hormone prescription. VA also said veterans with gender dysphoria would continue to receive comprehensive health care, including preventive and mental-health care. The department stated that it did not provide other medical or surgical therapy for gender dysphoria. The notice took effect upon publication on March 17. It supports a correction to the original date and scope, but by itself does not document individual treatment interruptions, lawsuits or outcomes for particular veterans.

supports: The March 17, 2025 VA notice rescinds Directive 1341(4), limits cross-sex hormone therapy to specified existing or separating veterans, says comprehensive preventive and mental-health care continues, and states the notice is effective on publication.

frozen_original.title: Trump Fires All Federal DEI Officers Overnight
frozen_original.synopsis: On January 20, 2025, the Trump administration placed all federal DEI officers — employees across more than 40 federal agencies whose job was to ensure equal opportunity in federal hiring, contracting, and services — on paid administrative leave and subsequently moved to terminate their positions. Hundreds of federal employees across agencies including the Department of Defense, Department of Education, and the intelligence community lost their positions overnight. The administration directed all agency heads to close their DEI offices within 30 days. Employees were instructed not to report to work and to return government equipment. Career civil servants who had worked in equal employment opportunity roles for years described receiving summary dismissal notices with no explanation. Unions representing federal workers filed grievances and legal challenges.

proposed_title: Trump revokes federal-contractor affirmative-action requirements in EO 14173
description_short: Trump revokes federal-contractor affirmative-action requirements in EO 14173
description_medium: Trump signed Executive Order 14173 on January 21, 2025. It revoked Executive Order 11246, which had imposed affirmative-action requirements on federal contractors, and directed agencies to add anti-discrimination-law compliance terms to federal contracts and grants. The text does not abolish every affirmative-action, outreach, admissions or mentoring program at all federally funded institutions.
description_long: President Trump signed Executive Order 14173 on January 21, 2025. The order revoked Executive Order 11246, ending the prior federal-contractor affirmative-action framework after a 90-day transition, and directed agency heads to include terms requiring contractors and grant recipients to comply with applicable federal anti-discrimination laws and certify that they do not operate DEI programs violating those laws. The action changed federal contracting and grant conditions, but it did not automatically abolish all affirmative-action, outreach, pipeline, mentoring or admissions programs at every institution receiving federal funds. The Federal Register text establishes the administration’s directives; it does not show how each agency or recipient implemented them or determine the legality of every affected program.

proposed_title: Trump Orders Agencies to End Environmental-Justice Programs; EPA Later Places Staff on Leave
description_short: Trump’s January orders directed agencies to end environmental-justice programs where lawful; EPA placed 171 employees on leave in February.

On February 11, EPA said it had placed 171 environmental-justice and DEIA employees on administrative leave. These actions do not establish that every federal program, employee, or grant ended on January 20.
description_long:
On January 20, 2025, President Donald Trump signed an executive order directing agencies, to the maximum extent allowed by law, to terminate environmental-justice offices and positions, programs, initiatives, and certain grants or contracts. A separate order revoked earlier federal orders, including environmental-justice policies. These were directives for agency action and review; they do not by themselves show that every relevant office, program, employee, rule, or grant was immediately ended that day.

On February 11, the Environmental Protection Agency announced that it had placed 171 employees on administrative leave: 160 working in environmental justice and 11 in diversity, equity, inclusion, and accessibility. That personnel action documents one implementation step, not a complete shutdown of all federal environmental-justice work. The supplied sources also do not establish that all Biden-era rules were rescinded or that hundreds of millions of dollars in grants were canceled through the January order. The corrected account distinguishes the order’s scope and legal qualifier from later agency implementation, and avoids presenting subsequent staffing or grant actions as a single completed event on inauguration day. Details about other agencies and grant cancellations require separate evidence.

proposed_title: Trump and Congress Nullified the Fair Pay and Safe Workplaces Rule in March 2017
description_short: Trump signed H.J. Res. 37 on March 27, 2017, nullifying the contracting rule; EO 13782 that day revoked the underlying executive orders.
description_medium: On March 27, 2017, Trump signed H.J. Res. 37, which nullified the Fair Pay and Safe Workplaces Federal Acquisition Regulation rule under the Congressional Review Act. He also signed EO 13782, revoking the prior executive orders authorizing the policy. The Federal Acquisition Regulation was formally amended later in 2017. This was not a February 2025 action.
description_long: The Fair Pay and Safe Workplaces rule was nullified in March 2017, not rescinded in February 2025. The University of California, Santa Barbara’s American Presidency Project records that on March 27, 2017, President Trump signed H.J. Res. 37, which nullified the Federal Acquisition Regulation rule. The later Federal Register removal notice explains that the statute gave the rule no force or effect and that Executive Order 13782, signed the same day, revoked the earlier executive orders that had authorized the policy. The regulatory provisions were formally removed later in 2017. These records support the sequence of congressional disapproval, presidential signature, same-day executive-order revocation, and subsequent rule removal. They do not establish every practical effect claimed in the original account, including that agencies were barred from considering all labor-law compliance histories in every contracting context or that named companies received billions without accountability. Any such consequences need separate contract and implementation evidence. The corrected description states the documented legal actions without extending them to unsupported outcomes.

proposed_title: Trump Removes NLRB Member Gwynne Wilcox and General Counsel Jennifer Abruzzo
description_short: Trump removed NLRB member Gwynne Wilcox and General Counsel Jennifer Abruzzo on January 27, 2025.
description_medium: On January 27, 2025, President Trump removed NLRB member Gwynne Wilcox and General Counsel Jennifer Abruzzo. Reuters reported that Wilcox’s removal left the five-member Board without a quorum and unable to issue decisions. Abruzzo was the agency’s general counsel, not a Board member. The reporting does not support the claim that Trump fired every Board member or that all NLRB functions stopped.
description_long: On January 27, 2025, President Donald Trump removed National Labor Relations Board member Gwynne Wilcox and General Counsel Jennifer Abruzzo. Reuters reported that Wilcox’s removal deprived the five-member Board of a quorum, preventing it from issuing decisions. The NLRB had two other vacancies, so removing Wilcox affected the Board’s ability to act; Abruzzo held the separate role of general counsel and was not another Board member. The agency said no reason was given for the dismissals, and Wilcox challenged her removal in court. This was a consequential intervention in NLRB leadership, but it did not remove every sitting Board member. The supplied reporting supports a limit on Board decisions while it lacked a quorum, not the claim that all agency functions disappeared or that every pending labor case was frozen indefinitely. This corrected entry replaces the original January 20 date and blanket shutdown description with the specific removals and quorum consequence reported at the time. Later litigation and staffing developments are separate events and are not inferred here.

proposed_title: Trump Signs Order Enforcing Hyde Amendment Restrictions on Federal Abortion Funding
description_short: On January 24, 2025, Trump ordered agencies to enforce Hyde Amendment restrictions and revoked two Biden reproductive-health executive orders.
description_medium: On January 24, 2025, Trump signed an order directing agencies to enforce the Hyde Amendment and revoking two Biden abortion-access executive orders. OMB's later implementation guidance retained legally authorized exceptions for rape, incest, and life-saving care. The order did not eliminate those statutory exceptions or establish specific later denials of care.
description_long: On January 24, 2025, President Donald Trump signed an order directing federal agencies to enforce the Hyde Amendment and revoking Executive Orders 14076 and 14079, which had directed agencies to promote reproductive-health access. The White House order set a federal funding policy and instructed the Office of Management and Budget to issue implementation guidance. In a later memorandum, OMB described how agencies should apply the policy and retained exceptions when federal law authorizes payment for care involving rape, incest, or life-saving treatment, subject to applicable law. The order's signing date is January 24, not January 20. It did not eliminate those exceptions, as the original synopsis claimed. The order and memorandum document federal directives; they do not, by themselves, establish that a named patient was denied care or that access changed in a particular federal program. Those consequences require separate evidence. This account separates the executive order from the later implementation memo and states their scope without claiming specific patient outcomes.

proposed_title: Head Start Faces Funding Delays and Regional Office Closures, but Continues Operating
description_short: Reuters reported Head Start grant delays after five HHS regional offices closed; Congress funded the program for FY2025 and HHS said services would continue.
description_medium: Reuters reported in May 2025 that five HHS regional offices overseeing Head Start had closed, delaying grant processing and straining some local programs. It cited a Democratic estimate that DOGE had released $943 million less in approved funding through April 15 than in the prior-year period. Congress had appropriated $12.27 billion for FY2025, and HHS said office closures would not reduce services; Head Start was not ended in March.
description_long:
Reuters reported on May 20, 2025, that Head Start programs were facing grant-processing delays and operational strain after five Department of Health and Human Services regional offices overseeing the program closed. The report described local providers coping with the disruptions; it did not say the national program had ended or that thousands of centers had received termination notices.

Reuters also cited congressional Democrats’ estimate that DOGE had released $943 million less in congressionally approved funding through April 15 than during the same period a year earlier. That comparison concerns funds released by that date and does not, by itself, establish a permanent cut to the enacted appropriation. Congress had appropriated $12.27 billion for Head Start in fiscal year 2025, and HHS said the regional office closures would not reduce services. Reuters reported that the program served nearly 800,000 children and supported 17,711 centers.

The evidence therefore supports a report about funding delays and administrative disruption, not termination of Head Start in March 2025 or an expected nationwide closure of centers. The cited article does not establish the number of individual centers that closed or the effects on specific children. This entry preserves those limits while correcting the event date to the Reuters report and the scope to continuing program operations.

description_long: In late April 2025, Reuters reported that DOGE had ordered the cancellation of about $400 million in AmeriCorps grants, citing a Washington Post report. These developments show major reductions and a legal challenge. Nor do the reports prove that every grant, placement, or service program ended permanently. The corrected account focuses on the grant actions and the states’ challenge, and it distinguishes reported cancellations from allegations made in litigation. The cited coverage does not resolve the status of each grant or the ultimate outcome of the case; those details require separate agency records and court filings.

description_long: On March 6, 2006, Donald Trump and his daughter Ivanka appeared on ABC’s The View to discuss her role as an adviser on The Apprentice. proposed_title: CNN Counted 404 Uses of the Word “Fake” by Trump in His First Year
description_short: CNN Counted 404 Uses of the Word “Fake” by Trump in His First Year
description_medium: CNNMoney reported on January 17, 2018, that Trump had used the word “fake” at least 404 times in tweets and public appearances since January 20, 2017. Its count included “fake news,” “fake media,” “fake polls” and other uses; it is not a count of the exact phrase “fake news” or a full first-term total. CNN said it used Factba.se and cross-checked other tools.
description_long: CNNMoney’s January 17, 2018 article reported that Donald Trump used the word “fake” at least 404 times in tweets and public appearances since his inauguration on January 20, 2017. The article said its count drew on Factba.se, a database of Trump’s speeches, interviews and tweets, and was corroborated with other tools, including Twitter search. It gave examples such as “fake news,” “fake polls,” “fake media” and “fake stories,” so the figure counts the word “fake” across multiple phrases rather than only the exact expression “fake news.” The count ends in January 2018 and cannot support the original entry’s claim of more than 2,000 exact-phrase uses during the full first term. Nor does this article alone prove a specific intent behind every use, effects on audiences, or that foreign leaders copied Trump because of it. Those broader claims require separate sources and attribution.

proposed_title: Trump Calls Former National Security Adviser John Bolton a “Dope” During Memoir Dispute
description_short: Trump calls former national security adviser John Bolton a “dope” during memoir dispute
description_medium: On June 18, 2020, Trump called former national security adviser John Bolton a “dope” during a public dispute over Bolton’s forthcoming memoir. Bolton had left the administration in September 2019, months earlier. The source documents the insult and timing; it does not establish that the remark was intended to deter cooperation with investigations.
description_long: On June 18, 2020, President Donald Trump publicly attacked former national security adviser John Bolton amid a dispute over Bolton’s forthcoming memoir. The Los Angeles Times reported that Trump called Bolton a “dope” and described the exchange as part of a wider argument over the former aide’s account of his time in the administration. Bolton had left the White House in September 2019, so the insult came months after his departure rather than immediately after it. The event date should therefore be June 18, 2020, not September 11, 2019. The article documents the public remark and its timing in the memoir dispute. It does not establish that Trump’s criticism was designed to deter cooperation with investigators, nor does the insult by itself prove claims about the memoir’s contents. Those claims require the memoir and other records to be assessed on their own evidence. This entry records the dated public attack and context without assigning a motive that the cited report does not demonstrate. The distinction keeps the well-sourced remark separate from unsupported claims about intimidation, investigations, or the substance of Bolton’s account.

proposed_title: House Democrats Report $7.8 Million in Foreign-Government Payments to Trump Properties
description_short: House Democrats Report $7.8 Million in Foreign-Government Payments to Trump Properties
description_medium: Records later obtained by congressional investigators showed that foreign governments made millions of dollars in payments to Trump-owned businesses while Donald Trump was president. House Oversight Democrats reported at least $7.8 million from 20 governments through four properties. Lawsuits and congressional reports argued that such payments implicated the Foreign Emoluments Clause, but the litigation did not produce a final merits judgment establishing a constitutional violation. The legal conclusion should therefore be attributed rather than stated as adjudicated fact.
description_long: House Oversight Democrats reported that records showed at least $7.8 million in payments from 20 foreign governments through four Trump properties during two years of Donald Trump’s presidency. The committee’s Democratic minority staff described this as its documented finding; it is a bounded amount from the records reviewed, not a comprehensive total for every Trump business or every year of the presidency. The payments raised Foreign Emoluments Clause questions, and lawsuits alleged constitutional violations. The Supreme Court dockets for Trump v. CREW and Trump v. District of Columbia show that the cases were vacated and remanded for dismissal as moot after Trump left office. The Court did not issue a final merits ruling establishing that the Clause was violated. The available record supports reporting the payments and the legal allegations with attribution, but it does not establish a judicially proven constitutional violation, that foreign governments directed spending to obtain policy favors, or that Trump personally received every payment. Keep the committee’s figure and the court outcomes distinct.

frozen_original.title: Trump Branded Properties Profit in Countries Seeking U.S. Favors: India, Philippines, Turkey
frozen_original.synopsis: Trump's international business interests created documented conflicts of interest across multiple countries where leaders and governments were simultaneously seeking U.S. policy favors. In India, Trump-branded luxury towers were being developed by the Lodha Group while the Modi government sought U.S. trade and defense concessions. In the Philippines, developer Century Properties was building Trump Tower Manila while President Rodrigo Duterte—whom Trump publicly praised—sought favorable U.S. treatment despite conducting extrajudicial killings. In Turkey, Trump Towers Istanbul generated licensing fees while Erdogan lobbied for concessions. In each case, local developers and governments had financial arrangements with Trump that created obvious incentives for the U.S. president to adopt favorable policies—precisely the conflict the Emoluments Clause was designed to prevent.

proposed_title: House Oversight Estimates $3.7 Million in Foreign Payments to Trump’s D.C. Hotel
description_short: House Oversight estimated foreign governments paid $3.7 million to Trump’s Washington hotel from 2017 to 2020; it was not a court finding.
description_medium: A House Oversight Committee investigation estimated that foreign governments paid about $3.7 million to the Trump International Hotel in Washington from 2017 through 2020. The committee said the payments raised possible Foreign Emoluments Clause concerns. This is the committee’s estimate and legal concern, not a judicial finding. The cited release does not support attributing a “$4M+” estimate specifically to CREW.
description_long:
A House Oversight Committee investigation estimated that foreign governments paid about $3.7 million to the Trump International Hotel in Washington between 2017 and 2020. In its October 8, 2021 release, the committee said its analysis of documents obtained from the General Services Administration showed payments during Donald Trump’s presidency. Committee leaders said the estimate raised concerns about possible violations of the Foreign Emoluments Clause.

The $3.7 million figure is the committee’s estimate, not a judicial determination that the Constitution was violated. The source does not validate the original record’s attribution of a “$4M+” estimate to Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington (CREW), nor does it establish that every payment had the same purpose or was unlawful. The entry therefore attributes the amount and constitutional concern to the House investigation. It describes the committee’s findings and argument without converting them into a court ruling or claiming the investigation proved an unlawful exchange.

proposed_title: Trump campaign paid more than $1 million to Trump Tower for office rent
description_short: Trump campaign paid more than $1 million to Trump Tower for office rent
description_medium: Politico reported from 2016 campaign-finance filings that the Trump campaign paid more than $1 million to Trump Tower to rent office space for its headquarters. HuffPost documented a rise in monthly rent from about $35,000 in March to $169,758 in July. The available reports do not establish the lease’s market value or prove that the payments were an overcharge.
description_long: Federal Election Commission filings reviewed by Politico show that Donald Trump’s 2016 campaign paid more than $1 million to Trump Tower for campaign-headquarters office space. HuffPost separately reported that monthly rent rose from about $35,000 in March 2016 to $169,758 in July. These reports document campaign payments to a Trump-owned property and a change in reported monthly rent. They do not establish the relevant lease terms or comparable market prices, so they do not prove the $1.7 million figure was an above-market overcharge or improper transfer. The evidence also does not establish that donor contributions flowed improperly to Trump personally or that this example proves a broader pattern during his presidency.

proposed_title: Ivanka Trump Merchandise Imports Rose 166% as Brand Sales Reached Record Levels
description_short: Ivanka Trump Merchandise Imports Rose 166%; Brand Sales Hit Record Levels
description_medium: An Associated Press report published April 18, 2017, said U.S. imports of Ivanka Trump merchandise, almost all from China, rose an estimated 166% in 2016 while the brand's sales reached record levels. It separately reported provisional Chinese approvals for three trademarks on April 6. The import statistic is not a sales or profit increase.
description_long: An Associated Press report published in April 2017 said U.S. imports of Ivanka Trump merchandise, almost all from China, had risen an estimated 166% over the prior year. The same report said the brand’s sales reached record levels in 2017. The 166% figure concerns imports; it is not a reported increase in sales or profits. The article also reported that on April 6, 2017, the Chinese government provisionally approved three new trademarks for Ivanka Trump’s company. These are separate business developments that drew scrutiny while she was beginning a White House role. The reporting does not establish that her government service or a particular trade-policy decision caused the rise in imports, record sales, or trademark approvals. Nor does it quantify the brand’s profits. The corrected account preserves the reported commercial activity and the timing of the trademark approvals while distinguishing the import statistic from sales growth. These facts explain the conflict-of-interest questions raised at the time, but they do not by themselves prove that government action produced commercial benefits or that a law was violated.

proposed_title: FEC Split 3–3 on Trump Campaign Vendor Payment Disclosure Allegations
description_short: The FEC split 3–3 on campaign-vendor disclosure allegations and later closed the matter; it made no criminal-fraud finding against Brad Parscale.
description_medium: FEC Matter Under Review 7784 concerned whether Trump campaign committees accurately reported payments to American Made Media Consultants and Parscale Strategy. The Commission split 3–3 on whether to find reason to believe certain reporting violations occurred; it later voted 4–2 to close the file. The record does not establish that Brad Parscale committed criminal fraud or personally received $40 million.
description_long:
Federal Election Commission Matter Under Review 7784 concerned complaints that Trump campaign committees misreported the payees or purposes of payments to American Made Media Consultants and Parscale Strategy. The Commission split 3–3 on whether to find reason to believe certain reporting violations occurred, so those allegations did not receive the necessary votes for that finding. The Commission later voted 4–2 to close the file.

The FEC’s public case page records the votes. The attached statements of reasons show that commissioners disagreed: three commissioners explained their decision to dismiss the reporting allegations, while two commissioners issued a separate statement criticizing the Commission’s handling. Those are commissioners’ positions, not a unanimous factual finding. The matter did not establish that Brad Parscale personally committed criminal fraud or pocketed $40 million. The corrected account describes the vendor-payment disclosure dispute and divided enforcement outcome without presenting a complaint, a commissioner’s statement or reported asset purchases as proof of personal fraud. The cited FEC record also does not establish the original claim that the personal purchases were proceeds of a fraudulent transfer.

proposed_title: Patel’s Past Rhetoric Raises Questions About FBI Independence
description_short: At his 2025 confirmation hearing, senators questioned Kash Patel about past remarks; the report does not show an FBI dossier program.
description_medium: During Kash Patel’s January 2025 confirmation hearing, senators questioned him about past comments concerning investigations of government officials and news media. Reuters reported that scrutiny of his rhetoric but did not describe FBI dossiers on Trump critics, expanded surveillance, or an operational change at the bureau. Evidence of those alleged activities would require FBI records or separate credible reporting identifying the targets and program.
description_long:
During Kash Patel’s confirmation process to lead the FBI, senators questioned him about past comments concerning investigations of government officials and news media. A Reuters report carried by Yahoo News describes the hearing and the scrutiny of Patel’s rhetoric, including questions about retribution and investigations of officials and journalists. Patel told senators that FBI investigations under his leadership would have a factual and legal basis.

The hearing provides evidence of questions about a nominee’s stated views; it does not establish that the FBI created dossiers on people who criticized Donald Trump, expanded domestic surveillance against them, or changed its operations. The original claim asserted a broad dossier and monitoring program, but the cited report describes no such activity. Claims about actual FBI operations require different evidence, such as an order, investigative records, or credible reporting that identifies the targets and the program. None is supplied here. The corrected account therefore preserves the confirmation-hearing scrutiny while distinguishing it from an unsupported allegation about bureau conduct. It does not claim that Patel’s statements resolved those concerns or that any resulting operational policy had already taken effect.

proposed_title: NBC Reports DHS Task Force Reviewed Foreign Students’ Social-Media Histories for Potential Visa Revocation
description_short: NBC reported on April 9, 2025, that a DHS task force was reviewing foreign students’ social media for potential visa-revocation grounds.
description_medium: NBC News reported on April 9, 2025, that a DHS task force was using data tools to review social-media histories of an estimated 1.5 million foreign students for potential grounds to revoke visas. The report describes screening and possible visa decisions; it does not identify a person deported in March because of an old post or establish that political criticism caused a completed removal.
description_long: NBC News reported on April 9, 2025, citing people familiar with the operation, that a newly created Department of Homeland Security task force was using data-analytic tools to review social-media histories of an estimated 1.5 million foreign students for potential grounds to revoke visas. The report also described review of records for charges or criminal convictions and stated that officials were considering certain online activity in immigration-benefit decisions. This is a report about screening and possible visa revocation, not evidence that a particular person was deported because of a years-old post. The original entry gives March 2025 as the event date and states that political criticism caused completed deportations, but the cited NBC report does not establish either point. It also does not adjudicate whether any screening practice was unconstitutional or prove the claimed chilling effect. This correction keeps the reported April screening operation separate from March enforcement cases, later H-1B/H-4 visa screening, and individual outcomes. Those matters require their own dated sources and case-specific evidence.

proposed_title: Reporting Describes DOGE Access to Sensitive HHS Systems and a Child-Support Database
description_short: Reports describe DOGE access to sensitive HHS systems and child-support data, not unrestricted access to complete medical records.
description_medium: Reporting based on HHS court filings said DOGE affiliates had access to 19 sensitive HHS systems; WIRED noted one instance apparently lacked required security training. The Washington Post separately reported read-only access to a child-support database containing income information. These reports raise access and privacy concerns but do not establish unrestricted access to millions of people’s complete medical records, diagnoses or prescriptions.
description_long: In March and April 2025, reporting described DOGE affiliates’ access to sensitive systems at the Department of Health and Human Services. WIRED, citing court filings and depositions, reported access to 19 systems, including financial and program databases, and said one affiliate apparently lacked required security training for a particularly sensitive system. The Washington Post separately reported that DOGE associates received read-only access to a child-support database containing income information, despite objections from career employees. Together, these reports document access to multiple government systems and raise questions about safeguards. They do not establish that DOGE had unrestricted access to complete medical records for millions of Americans, including HIV status, mental-health diagnoses or prescription histories. Nor do they show that every affiliate saw every record, that access was universally unauthorized, or that data was misused. Those stronger claims would require records identifying the systems and fields available to particular users, evidence about authorization and audit controls, and proof of actual access. This correction reports the scope the articles describe and preserves the evidence gap around detailed clinical records rather than repeating the original claim of carte-blanche access.

proposed_title: ICE adds cell-site-simulator vehicles through an $825,000 contract modification
corrected_claim: TechCrunch reported on October 7, 2025, that Immigration and Customs Enforcement had paid $825,000 earlier that year for a contract modification covering additional cell-site-simulator vehicles. Public records described the May 8 award as a modification for additional vehicles supporting the Homeland Security Technical Operations program. The same vendor had signed a similar ICE contract in September 2024, before the Trump administration. Cell-site simulators imitate cell towers and can be used to detect or locate nearby phones, but a procurement record establishes equipment funding rather than operational practice. The article does not identify how often or where the additional vehicles were deployed, which people were targeted, what authorization applied to a particular use, or how information from nearby devices was handled. It therefore does not support the original claim of broad warrantless surveillance across immigrant neighborhoods or a proven Fourth Amendment violation. The corrected account records the documented purchase while leaving deployment and warrant questions unresolved.

proposed_title: State Department Expands Online Vetting for Student and Exchange Visitor Visas
description_short: In June 2025, the State Department expanded online-presence screening for F, M, and J visa applicants; social-media identifiers were already collected under a 2019 policy.
description_medium: The State Department began requesting social-media identifiers from most U.S. visa applicants worldwide in 2019. In June 2025, it directed more comprehensive online-presence screening for F, M, and J student and exchange-visitor visa applicants as appointments resumed, and asked applicants to make profiles public. These distinct policies do not support the original claim of a January 20 order covering every applicant.
description_long: The 2025 student-visa screening directive was not the start of social-media collection for all U.S. visa applicants. The State Department said it began requesting social-media identifiers from most immigrant and nonimmigrant applicants worldwide in 2019, including identifiers used during the preceding five years. In June 2025, as student and exchange-visitor appointments resumed, the department directed more comprehensive online-presence review for applicants in the F, M, and J visa categories and asked them to make social-media profiles public for review. The measures have different dates and scopes: the older policy requested identifiers from most visa applicants, while the 2025 directive added screening for specified student and exchange-visitor categories. The cited sources do not support a January 20, 2025 executive order requiring every applicant to provide five years of social-media history, nor do they establish that applicants were denied visas for protected political expression or that the policy primarily targeted people from Muslim-majority countries. Those claims should not be presented as fact without additional evidence.

proposed_title: DOJ Briefly Halts and Then Restores Funding for Immigration Legal-Orientation Programs
description_short: DOJ paused four immigration legal-orientation programs in January 2025, then restored their funding after nonprofit providers sued.
description_medium: On January 22, 2025, DOJ ordered four federally funded programs providing legal orientation and guidance in immigration proceedings to stop work. After nonprofit providers challenged the interruption in court, DOJ restored the funding, according to AP. These programs offered information and guidance; the report does not show that the government ended legal representation for all detained immigrants.
description_long:
On January 22, 2025, the Department of Justice issued a stop-work order affecting four federally funded programs that provide legal orientation and guidance to people involved in immigration proceedings, according to the Associated Press. The order interrupted work by those programs; it was not a general rule eliminating every detained immigrant’s ability to seek a lawyer.

Nonprofit providers challenged the interruption in court, and DOJ later reversed course and ordered funding restored. The linked report supports that sequence: a stop-work directive, a legal challenge by providers, and restoration of funds. The episode concerns programs that provide information and orientation in immigration courts and detention settings. It should not be described as the termination of all legal representation for detained immigrants.

The cited AP account does not establish that tens of thousands lost attorneys, that staff were instructed to block attorney-client communication, or that transfers to remote facilities defied nationwide court orders. Those claims require separate direct evidence. This correction narrows the event to the four program funding interruption and its reversal, while preserving the distinction between legal-orientation assistance and appointed counsel or broader access to private attorneys.

After nonprofit providers sued, DOJ ordered the programs’ funding restored.

evidence_gaps: The AP report supports the four-program stop-work order and funding restoration; the broader claims require separate evidence about counsel access, transfers, and court orders.
unsupported_original_claims: That the order ended legal representation for detained immigrants generally or left tens of thousands without attorneys.
The claims about blocked attorney-client communications, remote transfers, or defied nationwide court orders.

proposed_title: Noem and Miller discuss possible habeas suspension in May 2025
description_short: In May 2025, Noem and Miller publicly discussed a possible habeas suspension; the reports describe consideration, not implementation.
description_medium: On May 14, 2025, Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem said recent immigration levels could provide a legal rationale for suspending habeas corpus. Stephen Miller had said days earlier that the administration was actively considering the option. The reports document discussion, not an implemented March policy ending habeas protections or directing officials to disregard petitions.
description_long: On May 14, 2025, Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem said she believed recent levels of illegal immigration could provide a legal rationale for suspending habeas corpus. White House adviser Stephen Miller had said days earlier that the administration was actively considering the option. The reports document public discussion of a possible suspension, not an implemented policy ending judicial review for detained immigrants. Noem expressed a view about a potential legal basis; the sources do not show that a court accepted it or that the administration issued an order. Miller’s comment indicated consideration rather than a final decision. The cited reporting describes no March directive to disregard habeas petitions, transfer detainees to evade favorable rulings, or contempt findings against officials. The correction therefore replaces the original claim of a completed March action with the later, sourced discussion while leaving any subsequent policy or effect on detention cases to separate evidence.

proposed_title: Trump Signs Order Labeling Antifa a 'Domestic Terrorist Organization'
description_short: Trump Signs Order Labeling Antifa a 'Domestic Terrorist Organization'
description_medium: On September 22, 2025, Trump signed an order labeling Antifa a domestic terrorist organization and directing agencies to investigate illegal operations conducted on its behalf. The label’s legal effect is uncertain because federal law has no domestic designation process equivalent to the one for foreign terrorist groups. The order did not itself make nonviolent protest a crime.
description_long: On September 22, 2025, Donald Trump signed an executive order labeling Antifa a domestic terrorist organization. The order directed federal agencies to use existing authorities to investigate, disrupt, and dismantle illegal operations carried out by people acting on Antifa’s behalf, including certain material-support activity. It did not create a separate domestic designation system or make association with Antifa a crime. Federal law provides a formal process for designating foreign terrorist organizations, but not an equivalent mechanism for domestic groups, leaving the practical legal force of the label uncertain. The directive focused on illegal activity and existing authorities rather than expressly criminalizing peaceful protest. The distinction matters because a presidential label does not by itself establish that every protester or person associated with a decentralized movement committed an offense. The order prompted debate about how agencies could use current law and what constitutional limits apply when political activity is described as terrorism. The public record cited here does not establish a subsequent wave of terrorism prosecutions resulting from the order.

proposed_title: USCIS Implements Registration and Fingerprinting Requirements for Certain Noncitizens
corrected_claim: USCIS describes registration requirements for certain previously unregistered noncitizens who remain in the United States for 30 days or longer; fingerprints are required where applicable under law. The cited process is not evidence of universal enrollment in a new DHS biometric database or collection of DNA, iris scans, and facial geometry.
description_short: USCIS describes registration and fingerprinting requirements for certain previously unregistered noncitizens.
description_medium: USCIS describes registration requirements for certain noncitizens age 14 or older who were not previously registered and who remain in the United States for at least 30 days. The process uses Form G-325R, with fingerprints where required by law. The cited page does not establish a new universal database or collection of DNA, iris scans, and facial geometry from every undocumented immigrant.
description_long: The U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services page describes the federal alien-registration requirement for certain noncitizens who were not previously registered and who remain in the United States for at least 30 days. It identifies age and prior-registration categories and explains that Form G-325R is used for registration, with fingerprints when required by law. The page documents a registration process; it does not establish that DHS created a new comprehensive database for every undocumented immigrant. It also does not support the frozen entry’s claims that the process universally collects facial geometry, iris scans, or DNA, or that records would be shared with authoritarian governments. description_long: President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14243, “Stopping Waste, Fraud, and Abuse by Eliminating Information Silos,” on March 20, 2025; it was published in the Federal Register on March 25. The order directs agencies, to the maximum extent consistent with law, to facilitate access to and sharing of unclassified agency records, data, software, and systems for administration priorities involving waste, fraud, and abuse. It also calls for review of guidance and regulations that may impede sharing. The order’s text does not repeal the Privacy Act of 1974 or eliminate all federal privacy protections, and its direction is expressly bounded by applicable law. The actual records shared, recipients, safeguards, and effects depend on agency implementation and relevant legal obligations. The corrected entry therefore describes a directive and review process rather than asserting that unrestricted access to all personal records occurred or that a comprehensive surveillance system was created. The cited order supports its date and stated scope; evidence about a specific transfer or privacy violation would need to identify the agency, data, and action involved.

frozen_original.title: Trump ends privacy protections in federal data collection
frozen_original.synopsis: Trump signed an executive order eliminating existing privacy protections governing federal data collection programs, opening Americans personal data to broader government use without consent. The order gutted regulations implementing the Privacy Act of 1974, which had required agencies to tell citizens what data they were collecting and how it would be used. The elimination of these protections enabled the creation of a comprehensive federal surveillance infrastructure combining data from dozens of agencies without any notice to affected citizens.

proposed_title: Trump Announces Stargate AI Infrastructure Venture With Up to $500 Billion Planned Investment
description_short: Trump announced Stargate, a private-sector AI venture with up to $500 billion in planned U.S. investment.
description_medium: At the White House on January 21, 2025, Trump joined OpenAI, SoftBank and Oracle leaders to announce Stargate, a private-sector AI infrastructure venture planning up to $500 billion in U.S. investment over four years. The announcement was not an executive order, and the full amount was a plan, not money already deployed.
description_long: President Donald Trump announced the Stargate AI infrastructure venture at the White House on January 21, 2025, with leaders from OpenAI, SoftBank and Oracle. The companies said they planned to invest up to $500 billion in U.S. infrastructure over four years. The amount described a prospective plan, not $500 billion already spent. The announcement concerned a private-sector business venture and was not an executive order. The project brought together technology and investment companies around plans for data centers and computing capacity intended to support artificial intelligence. The Reuters report documents the announcement and the companies’ stated investment plan. It does not establish that SoftBank received favorable regulatory treatment in exchange for the pledge. It also does not verify separate statements by Elon Musk about the financing or a resulting dispute with Sam Altman; those are distinct claims and would need sources covering them. The supported event is the launch announcement and prospective investment commitment, without treating planned spending as completed or implying a government bargain.

proposed_title: Trump Signs Childhood-Vaccine Order and Discusses Autism in August 2026 Remarks
description_short: Trump signed a childhood-vaccine order on August 10, 2026, and made autism-related remarks; WHO's review found no causal link.
description_medium: On August 10, 2026, President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14420 revising federal childhood-vaccine recommendations, including separate MMR components when available and spacing visits. At the signing, he discussed autism. A WHO review of evidence through 2025 found that rigorous studies do not support a causal association between vaccines and autism. The order and the scientific evidence are distinct.
description_long: On August 10, 2026, President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14420, which directs changes to federal childhood-vaccine recommendations, including separate administration of measles, mumps, and rubella components when available and spacing some immunizations across visits. At the signing, Trump discussed autism and childhood vaccination. The executive order documents a policy action and the presidential transcript records his remarks; neither is scientific evidence that vaccines cause autism. The World Health Organization's review of evidence through 2025 found that the most methodologically rigorous studies do not support a causal association between vaccines, including thiomersal-containing vaccines, and autism spectrum disorder. The order was signed by Trump, not by Robert F. Kennedy Jr. This correction therefore changes the event date from 2025 to August 10, 2026, distinguishes the order's recommendations from the president's rhetoric, and separates both from the scientific evidence. It does not treat the signing itself as proof of a vaccine-autism link.
